title: DEEP BATCH ACTIVE LEARNING BY DIVERSE, UNCERTAIN GRADIENT LOWER BOUNDS

elements.name: Pool-based active learning setting
elements.description: The learner selects unlabeled pool examples for label queries and seeks low classification error with few queries.
elements.source_text: We consider the pool-based active learning setup, where the learner receives an unlabeled dataset U sampled according to  $D_{\mathcal X}$  and can request labels sampled according to  $D_{\mathcal Y|\mathcal X}$  for any  $x\in U$ .
elements.pseudocode: Maintain unlabeled pool U and labeled set S; select pool points, query labels, then train on S.

elements.name: Neural classifier prediction
elements.description: The classifier chooses the class with the largest output probability.
elements.source_text: $h_{\theta}(x) = \operatorname{argmax}_{y \in [K]} f(x; \theta)_y$
elements.pseudocode: y_hat = argmax(f(x; theta))

elements.name: Cross-entropy training loss
elements.description: The neural classifier is trained by minimizing cross-entropy over labeled examples.
elements.source_text: $\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}(p, y) = \sum_{i=1}^K I(y=i) \ln 1/p_i = \ln 1/p_y$ .
elements.pseudocode: cross_entropy(p, y) = -log(p[y])

elements.name: BADGE batch active learning
elements.description: BADGE repeatedly embeds unlabeled points with hallucinated last-layer gradients, selects a diverse batch, queries labels, and retrains.
elements.source_text: BADGE, described in Algorithm 1 starts by drawing an initial set of M examples uniformly at random from U and asking for their labels. It then proceeds iteratively, performing two main computations at each step t: a gradient embedding computation and a sampling computation.
elements.pseudocode: Initialize S with M random labeled pool examples. Train theta on S. For each round: predict y_hat and compute g_x for each unlabeled x; choose B embeddings with k-means++ seeding; query their labels; add them to S; retrain theta from scratch. Return theta.

elements.name: Hallucinated gradient embedding computation
elements.description: For every unlabeled point, use the model's predicted label as a surrogate label and compute the cross-entropy gradient with respect to the output layer.
elements.source_text: Compute gradient embedding  $g_x = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_{\text{out}}} \ell_{\text{CE}}(f(x;\theta), \hat{y}(x))|_{\theta=\theta_t}$ , where  $\theta_{\text{out}}$  refers to parameters of the final (output) layer.
elements.pseudocode: p = model(x); y_hat = argmax(p); g_x = gradient(cross_entropy(p, y_hat), output_layer_parameters)

elements.name: BADGE gradient embedding
elements.description: The acquisition embedding is the last-layer gradient of cross-entropy under the predicted label.
elements.source_text: $g_x = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_{\text{out}}} \ell_{\text{CE}}(f(x;\theta), \hat{y}(x))|_{\theta=\theta_t}$
elements.pseudocode: g_x = d/d(theta_out) cross_entropy(f(x; theta), y_hat(x)) evaluated at theta_t

elements.name: Gradient magnitude as uncertainty
elements.description: A large hallucinated gradient means the point may cause a large parameter update; confident points have small embedding norms.
elements.source_text: we consider the model uncertain about an example if knowing the label induces a large gradient of the loss with respect to the model parameters and hence a large update to the model.
elements.pseudocode: uncertainty(x) = norm(g_x)

elements.name: Softmax cross-entropy at the final layer
elements.description: Cross-entropy is expressed in terms of final-layer weights and penultimate representation.
elements.source_text: $$\ell_{\text{CE}}(f(x;\theta), y) = \ln \left( \sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{W_j \cdot z(x;V)} \right) - W_y \cdot z(x;V).$$
elements.pseudocode: loss = log(sum_j(exp(dot(W_j, z)))) - dot(W_y, z)

elements.name: Per-class gradient embedding block
elements.description: For softmax classification, each output-class block combines the predicted-label residual with the penultimate representation.
elements.source_text: $$(g_x)_i = \frac{\partial}{\partial W_i} \ell_{CE}(f(x;\theta), \hat{y}) = (p_i - I(\hat{y} = i))z(x; V). \tag{1}$$
elements.pseudocode: g_x[i] = (p[i] - indicator(y_hat == i)) * z(x; V) for each class i

elements.name: Predicted-label gradient is a lower bound
elements.description: The predicted label minimizes the last-layer gradient norm over candidate labels, so the embedding conservatively estimates possible update magnitude.
elements.source_text: Consequently,  $\hat{y} = \operatorname{argmin}_{y \in [K]} \|g_x^y\|$ .
elements.pseudocode: Verify experimentally that norm(g_x using argmax class) is no greater than gradients using other classes.

elements.name: Last-layer gradient norm
elements.description: The norm depends on the class probabilities, selected label, and penultimate representation norm.
elements.pseudocode: gradient_norm_sq(y) = (sum_i(p[i]^2) + 1 - 2*p[y]) * norm(z)^2

elements.name: k-MEANS++ seeding over gradient embeddings
elements.description: Select the first gradient embedding uniformly, then repeatedly sample candidates proportional to squared distance from the nearest selected embedding.
elements.source_text: k-MEANS++ seeding selects centroids by iteratively sampling points in proportion to their squared distances from the nearest centroid that has already been chosen, which, like a k-DPP, tends to select a diverse batch of high-magnitude samples.
elements.pseudocode: Choose first center uniformly. Until B centers: D(x) = min distance from x to chosen centers; sample x with probability D(x)^2 / sum_u D(u)^2; add x.

elements.name: Nearest-center distance
elements.description: The candidate distance is its Euclidean distance to the closest selected center.
elements.pseudocode: D_t(x) = min(norm(x - c, 2) for c in C)

elements.name: k-MEANS++ sampling probability
elements.description: Each subsequent center is sampled in proportion to squared nearest-center distance.
elements.source_text: c_t \leftarrow \text{Sample } x \text{ from } G \text{ with probability } \frac{D_t(x)^2}{\sum_{x \in G} D_t(x)^2}.
elements.pseudocode: sample x from G with weights D_t(x)^2

elements.name: Joint diversity and uncertainty acquisition
elements.description: Embedding norm captures uncertainty while k-MEANS++ distances discourage redundant selections, yielding high-magnitude and directionally diverse batches without tuning a trade-off.
elements.source_text: We want the newly-acquired labeled samples to induce large and diverse changes to the model.
elements.pseudocode: Use gradient embeddings as k-means++ points so their norms and separation jointly affect selection.

elements.name: Expected k-means approximation diversity guarantee
elements.description: k-MEANS++ centers approximate the k-means objective in expectation, providing a theoretical rationale for diverse selection.
elements.source_text: It is shown in (Arthur and Vassilvitskii) 2007) that the set of centers returned is guaranteed to approximate the k-means objective function in expectation, thus ensuring diversity.

elements.name: Initial labeled pool size M
elements.description: The algorithm begins with M uniformly sampled labeled examples; experiments use M=100.
elements.source_text: we evaluate them in a batch-mode active learning setup with M=100 being the number of initial random labeled examples
elements.pseudocode: initial_size = 100

elements.name: Acquisition batch size B
elements.description: B is the number of unlabeled examples selected and queried in each active-learning round; experiments vary it over 100, 1000, and 10000.
elements.source_text: batch size B varying from  $\{100,1000,10000\}$ .

elements.name: Retraining after acquisition
elements.description: After each queried batch, models are retrained from scratch rather than warm-started.
elements.source_text: We avoid warm starting and retrain models from scratch every time new samples are queried
elements.pseudocode: After adding a queried batch to S, initialize a fresh model and train it on all of S.

elements.name: BADGE robustness evaluation
elements.description: The paper evaluates BADGE across datasets, architectures, and batch sizes using test accuracy versus queried labels.
elements.source_text: We evaluate the performance of BADGE against several algorithms from the literature. In our experiments, we seek to answer the following question: How robust are the learning algorithms to choices of neural network architecture, batch size, and dataset?
elements.pseudocode: For each selected dataset and batch size, run BADGE acquisition rounds, retrain, and record test accuracy against total queried labels.

elements.name: Experimental training protocol
elements.description: Models use Adam-variant SGD and cross-entropy until over 99 percent training accuracy; learning rates differ for image and non-image data.
elements.source_text: models using cross-entropy loss and the Adam variant of SGD until training accuracy exceeds 99%. We use a learning rate of 0*.*001 for image data and of 0*.*0001 for non-image data.
elements.pseudocode: Train with Adam and cross entropy until train accuracy > 0.99; learning_rate = 0.001 for image data or 0.0001 for non-image data.

elements.name: Empirical robustness across conditions
elements.description: BADGE is reported to perform similarly to or better than comparison approaches over different architectures and batch sizes.
elements.source_text: We have established that BADGE is empirically an effective deep active learning algorithm across different architectures and batch sizes, performing similar to or better than other active learning algorithms.
elements.pseudocode: Plot the single BADGE learning curve and report its accuracy as queried labels increase.
